reader.title: Grain Valley hanging
bases: An unidentified man was found dead by hanging in woods near Grain Valley; papers called it a lynching by train robbers or a vigilance committee but also suggested suicide, and none named a victim, perpetrators or race (A1, A2, A14).

A man died by hanging, but whether he was killed at all is disputed (A1 says 'no doubt' a lynching; A14 thinks suicide most likely), and no report identifies a group, its size, or a pretext beyond rival theories (vigilance committee punishment in A7, robbers silencing a detective in A9).

The finding of the body is reported independently from Independence (A1), St. Louis (A2) and Missouri (A14), but A14 contradicts the lynching claims of A1, A2 and A7 by judging suicide the most reasonable explanation.

summary.text: The Grain Valley hanging was the death of an unidentified man whose body was found hanging from a tree in woods near Grain Valley Station, Jackson County, Missouri, on October 15, 1881.

The man was never identified in the coverage, and newspapers offered competing explanations: that he was a detective lynched by train robbers, a suspect lynched by a vigilance committee or by farmers, or a suicide.
The story drew notice because Jackson County was then the scene of prosecutions for two train robberies, and the wire report that carried it was headlined "A Detective's Fate."
In mid-October 1881 the courts at Independence were dealing with the Glendale and Blue Cut train robberies.

The same Independence dispatch that first reported the body noted that William Ryan, convicted of taking part in the Glendale robbery, had been sentenced that day to twenty-five years in the penitentiary.
Within weeks a grand jury at Independence indicted three men for the Blue Cut robbery of September 7.
According to the New York Sun's correspondent, a vigilance committee was known to exist in that part of the county.
A farmer passing through a dense woods a few miles from Grain Valley found the body and gave the alarm.

A St. Louis dispatch placed the spot four miles from Grain Valley Station on the Chicago and Alton Railroad, some twenty miles from Kansas City, while the Martinsburg Independent put it twenty miles from Independence.
The Sun's dispatch said the man had been dead several days, and the St. Louis wire said the body had apparently been hanging for three days.
The Iron County Register described the scene differently: the body lay on the ground under the tree with a rope around the neck, while another piece of the same rope hung from a limb above.
Efforts to identify the dead man failed, and no report stated his race.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or an identification appears in the coverage, which ends in early November.
The story spread mainly through a short St. Louis wire item, headed "A Detective's Fate" in the Chicago Daily Tribune and "Fate of a Detective" in the Wheeling Register.
The same text ran nearly word for word in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Salt Lake Herald and the Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, and as late as October 27 in the Bolivar Bulletin.
That item presented as "the theory" that the man was a detective who had been lynched by someone connected with the recent train robbery.

A weekly news digest printed in the Mineral Point Tribune and the Grant County Herald gave another version, saying people near Independence were "greatly excited" and believed a vigilance committee had lynched the man for taking part in the Glendale robbery.

The Martinsburg Independent told the detective theory almost as fact, while a digest in the Democratic Messenger and the Connecticut Western News said only that opinion was divided whether the dead man was a train robber or a detective.
By October 25 the Daily Kennebec Journal had reduced the story to one line: "A supposed detective was found lynched near Kansas City, Mo."
Only the Iron County Register, a Missouri weekly, favored suicide, calling it "a very mysterious hanging" and suicide the "most reasonable" explanation.
None of the reports mentioned race, and the episode appears only in the white press.
Accounts disagreed on whether the death was a lynching at all.

The Sun's Independence dispatch said there seemed to be no doubt that a lynching had been done, though opinion was about equally divided between a vigilance committee and train robbers who had made away with a detective.
The Martinsburg Independent said the robber gang had captured the detective and "strung him up to prevent his hunting them down."
The Iron County Register listed both a detective killed by robbers and a horse thief punished by local farmers before judging suicide the most likely explanation.
The Register's account came later and from within Missouri, with the fullest description of the scene, but like the others it cited no inquest or named source.

framing.detail: Headlined 'A Detective's Fate' and 'Fate of a Detective', the St. Louis wire item presented the detective-lynching theory and ran nearly verbatim from Wheeling to Sacramento.
Digests told it either as a vigilance-committee lynching that had people 'greatly excited' or as an open question whether the dead man was train-robber or detective.
The Iron County Register called it 'a very mysterious hanging' and judged suicide the most reasonable explanation.
